content: The concept of the nadi system, as referenced in ancient texts, is first mentioned in the Chandogya Upanishad. This text identifies three primary nadis: Ida, Pingala, and Sushumna. The Sushumna nadi is described as the central channel that runs along the cerebrospinal axis, extending from the perineum to the cranial junction of the lambdoid and sagittal sutures. Ida, located on the left side, is associated with a pale color and negative polarity, while Pingala, on the right side, is linked to a red color and positive polarity. These three nadis are considered the most significant among the network of nadis, although some tantric texts suggest there are over 72,000 nadis branching out from the central chakras and becoming progressively finer as they extend outward. The Sat-Cakra-Narupana, one of the earliest texts on nadis and chakras, explicitly refers to these three main nadis, naming them Sasi (Ida), Mihira (Pingala), and Sushumna. It describes Sushumna as being composed of the three gunas (qualities) and positioned centrally. Sushumna is said to embody the forms of the Moon, Sun, and Fire, with its structure resembling a string of blooming Datura flowers. It extends from the Kanda (a subtle energy center near the base of the spine) to the head, with an inner channel called Vajra that shines and stretches from the Medhra (genital region) to the head. Nadis are believed to carry a vital life force energy known as prana in Sanskrit, or qi in Chinese systems. Prana, the active energy, is thought to flow through Pingala, while Apana, the passive energy, flows through Ida. When awakened, Kundalini energy is said to travel through the Sushumna nadi. Ida and Pingala are often associated with the two hemispheres of the brain. Pingala, the solar nadi, is linked to the right side of the body and the left hemisphere of the brain, representing extroverted and active qualities. Ida, the lunar nadi, corresponds to the left side of the body and the right hemisphere of the brain, symbolizing introverted and reflective qualities. These nadis cross at the optic chiasma, creating a connection between the brain and body. The nadis are also thought to have extrasensory functions, influencing empathetic and instinctive responses. They can be stimulated through practices such as Pranayama, which involves alternate nostril breathing. This technique alternates stimulation of the left and right sides of the brain, promoting balance and purification of the energetic currents. The term nadi originates from the Sanskrit root nad, meaning channel, stream, or flow. Rhythmic breathing and specialized techniques are believed to influence the flow of these nadis, purifying and developing them to awaken Kundalini energy. In some interpretations, particularly within mystical Western esotericism combined with yoga concepts, the three nadis are metaphorically linked to alchemical elements. Pingala is associated with alchemical sulfur, representing heat, dryness, and the Sun, while Ida is linked to alchemical mercury, symbolizing coldness, moisture, and the Moon. The imagery of two serpents coiling around a central rod, as seen in Eastern symbolism, corresponds to the intertwining of Pingala and Ida around the Merudanda (spinal column).
